- Full regex syntax (e.g. "log.*Error", "function\s+\w+"). Ripgrep, not grep — escape literal braces (`interface\{\}`).
- Filter with `glob` (e.g. "**/*.tsx") or `type` (e.g. "js", "py", "rust").
- `output_mode`: "content" (matching lines), "files_with_matches" (paths only, default), or "count".
- `multiline: true` for patterns that span lines.

pattern.description: The regular expression pattern to search for in file contents

path.description: File or directory to search in (rg PATH). Defaults to current working directory.

glob.description: Glob pattern to filter files (e.g. "*.js", "*.{ts,tsx}") - maps to rg --glob

output_mode.description: Output mode: "content" shows matching lines (supports -A/-B/-C context, -n line numbers, head_limit), "files_with_matches" shows file paths (supports head_limit), "count" shows match counts (supports head_limit). Defaults to "files_with_matches".

-B.description: Number of lines to show before each match (rg -B). Requires output_mode: "content", ignored otherwise.

-A.description: Number of lines to show after each match (rg -A). Requires output_mode: "content", ignored otherwise.

context.description: Number of lines to show before and after each match (rg -C). Requires output_mode: "content", ignored otherwise.

-n.description: Show line numbers in output (rg -n). Requires output_mode: "content", ignored otherwise. Defaults to true.

-o.description: Print only the matched (non-empty) parts of each matching line, one match per output line (rg -o / --only-matching). Requires output_mode: "content", ignored otherwise. Defaults to false.

type.description: File type to search (rg --type). Common types: js, py, rust, go, java, etc. More efficient than include for standard file types.

head_limit.description: Limit output to first N lines/entries, equivalent to "| head -N". Works across all output modes: content (limits output lines), files_with_matches (limits file paths), count (limits count entries). Defaults to 250 when unspecified. Pass 0 for unlimited (use sparingly — large result sets waste context).

offset.description: Skip first N lines/entries before applying head_limit, equivalent to "| tail -n +N | head -N". Works across all output modes. Defaults to 0.

multiline.description: Enable multiline mode where . matches newlines and patterns can span lines (rg -U --multiline-dotall). Default: false.

tools.name: PowerShell
tools.description:
Executes a given PowerShell command with optional timeout. Working directory persists between commands; shell state (variables, functions) does not.

IMPORTANT: This tool is for terminal operations via PowerShell: git, npm, docker, and PS cmdlets. DO NOT use it for file operations (reading, writing, editing, searching, finding files) - use the specialized tools for this instead.

PowerShell edition: PowerShell 7+ (pwsh)
   - Pipeline chain operators `&&` and `||` ARE available and work like bash. Prefer `cmd1 && cmd2` over `cmd1; cmd2` when cmd2 should only run if cmd1 succeeds.
   - Ternary (`$cond ? $a : $b`), null-coalescing (`??`), and null-conditional (`?.`) operators are available.
   - Default file encoding is UTF-8 without BOM.

Before executing the command, please follow these steps:

1. Directory Verification:
   - If the command will create new directories or files, first use `Get-ChildItem` (or `ls`) to verify the parent directory exists and is the correct location

2. Command Execution:
   - Always quote file paths that contain spaces with double quotes
   - Capture the output of the command.

PowerShell Syntax Notes:
   - Variables use $ prefix: $myVar = "value"
   - Escape character is backtick (`), not backslash
   - Use Verb-Noun cmdlet naming: Get-ChildItem, Set-Location, New-Item, Remove-Item
   - Common aliases: ls (Get-ChildItem), cd (Set-Location), cat (Get-Content), rm (Remove-Item)
   - Pipe operator | works similarly to bash but passes objects, not text
   - Use Select-Object, Where-Object, ForEach-Object for filtering and transformation
   - String interpolation: "Hello $name" or "Hello $($obj.Property)"
   - Registry access uses PSDrive prefixes: `HKLM:\SOFTWARE\...`, `HKCU:\...` — NOT raw `HKEY_LOCAL_MACHINE\...`
   - Environment variables: read with `$env:NAME`, set with `$env:NAME = "value"` (NOT `Set-Variable` or bash `export`)
   - Call native exe with spaces in path via call operator: `& "C:\Program Files\App\app.exe" arg1 arg2`

Unix commands that DO NOT exist in PowerShell — use the equivalent instead:
   - head / tail → `Get-Content file -TotalCount N` / `-Tail N`; piped: `| Select-Object -First N` / `-Last N`
   - which → `(Get-Command name).Source`
   - touch → `if (-not (Test-Path path)) { New-Item -ItemType File path }` (NEVER use `New-Item -Force` on a file — it truncates existing content)
   - wc -l → `(Get-Content file | Measure-Object -Line).Lines`
   - mkdir -p → `New-Item -ItemType Directory -Force path` (`-p` is not a PowerShell flag)
   - rm -rf → `Remove-Item -Recurse -Force path`
   - ln -s → `New-Item -ItemType SymbolicLink -Path link -Target target`
   - chmod / chown → not applicable on Windows; use `icacls` only if ACL changes are required
   - 2>/dev/null → `2>$null` (but stderr is captured for you — usually unnecessary)
   - VAR=x cmd → `$env:VAR = 'x'; cmd` (PowerShell has no inline env-var prefix)
   - Bash control flow (`if [ -f x ]`, `for x in *`, backtick ``cmd`` substitution) is a parser error — use `if (Test-Path x)`, `foreach ($x in ...)`, `$(cmd)`

Exit-code note: `-ErrorAction SilentlyContinue` suppresses error OUTPUT but the cmdlet failure still causes this tool to report exit 1. To make a cmdlet failure truly non-fatal, promote it to terminating and swallow it: `try { Cmdlet ... -ErrorAction Stop } catch {}` (without `-ErrorAction Stop`, non-terminating errors skip the `catch` and still exit 1).

Interactive and blocking commands (this tool runs with -NonInteractive and stdin attached to the null device — console prompts read EOF or error immediately; GUI prompts can still block until timeout):
   - NEVER use `Read-Host`, `Get-Credential`, `Out-GridView`, `$Host.UI.PromptForChoice`, or `pause`
   - Destructive cmdlets (`Remove-Item`, `Stop-Process`, `Clear-Content`, etc.) may prompt for confirmation. Add `-Confirm:$false` when you intend the action to proceed. Use `-Force` for read-only/hidden items.
   - Never use `git rebase -i`, `git add -i`, or other commands that open an interactive editor

Passing multiline strings (commit messages, file content) to native executables:
   - Use a single-quoted here-string so PowerShell does not expand `$` or backticks inside. The closing `'@` MUST be at column 0 (no leading whitespace) on its own line — indenting it is a parse error:
<example>
git commit -m @'
Commit message here.
Second line with $literal dollar signs.
'@
</example>
   - Use `@'...'@` (single-quoted, literal) not `@"..."@` (double-quoted, interpolated) unless you need variable expansion
   - For arguments containing `-`, `@`, or other characters PowerShell parses as operators, use the stop-parsing token: `git log --% --format=%H`

Usage notes:
  - The command argument is required.
  - You can specify an optional timeout in milliseconds (up to 600000ms / 10 minutes for a foreground command). If not specified, commands will timeout after 120000ms (2 minutes).
  - It is very helpful if you write a clear, concise description of what this command does.
  - If the output exceeds 30000 characters, output will be truncated before being returned to you.
  - You can use the `run_in_background` parameter to run the command in the background. Only use this if you don't need the result immediately and are OK being notified when the command completes later. You do not need to check the output right away - you'll be notified when it finishes.
  - Avoid using PowerShell to run commands that have dedicated tools, unless explicitly instructed:
    - File search: Use Glob (NOT Get-ChildItem -Recurse)
    - Content search: Use Grep (NOT Select-String)
    - Read files: Use Read (NOT Get-Content)
    - Edit files: Use Edit
    - Write files: Use Write (NOT Set-Content/Out-File)
    - Communication: Output text directly (NOT Write-Output/Write-Host)
  - When issuing multiple commands:
    - If the commands are independent and can run in parallel, make multiple PowerShell tool calls in a single message.
    - If the commands depend on each other and must run sequentially, chain them in a single PowerShell call (see edition-specific chaining syntax above).
    - Use `;` only when you need to run commands sequentially but don't care if earlier commands fail.
    - DO NOT use newlines to separate commands (newlines are ok in quoted strings and here-strings)
  - Do NOT prefix commands with `cd` or `Set-Location` -- the working directory is already set to the correct project directory automatically.
  - Avoid unnecessary `Start-Sleep` commands:
    - Do not sleep between commands that can run immediately — just run them.
    - If your command is long running and you would like to be notified when it finishes — simply run your command using `run_in_background`. There is no need to sleep in this case.
    - Do not retry failing commands in a sleep loop — diagnose the root cause or consider an alternative approach.
    - If waiting for a background task you started with `run_in_background`, you will be notified when it completes — do not poll.
    - If you must poll an external process, use a check command rather than sleeping first.
    - If you must sleep, keep the duration short to avoid blocking the user.
  - For git commands:
    - Prefer to create a new commit rather than amending an existing commit.
    - Before running destructive operations (e.g., git reset --hard, git push --force, git checkout --), consider whether there is a safer alternative that achieves the same goal. Only use destructive operations when they are truly the best approach.
    - Never skip hooks (--no-verify) or bypass signing (--no-gpg-sign, -c commit.gpgsign=false) unless the user has explicitly asked for it. If a hook fails, investigate and fix the underlying issue.

tools.name: Read
tools.description:
Reads a file from the local filesystem.

- `file_path` must be an absolute path.
- Reads up to 2000 lines by default.
- When you already know which part of the file you need, only read that part. This can be important for larger files.
- Results are returned using cat -n format, with line numbers starting at 1
- Reads images (PNG, JPG, …) and presents them visually. Reads PDFs via the `pages` parameter (e.g. "1-5", max 20 pages/request; required for PDFs over 10 pages). Reads Jupyter notebooks (.ipynb) as cells with outputs.
- Reading a directory, a missing file, or an empty file returns an error or system reminder rather than content.
- Do NOT re-read a file you just edited to verify — Edit/Write would have errored if the change failed, and the harness tracks file state for you.

- When you already know which part of the file you need, only read that part. This can be important for larger files.
- Results are returned using cat -n format, with line numbers starting at 1
- Reads images (PNG, JPG, …) and presents them visually. Reads PDFs via the `pages` parameter (e.g. "1-5", max 20 pages/request; required for PDFs over 10 pages). Reads Jupyter notebooks (.ipynb) as cells with outputs.
- Reading a directory, a missing file, or an empty file returns an error or system reminder rather than content.
- Do NOT re-read a file you just edited to verify — Edit/Write would have errored if the change failed, and the harness tracks file state for you.

pages.description: Page range for PDF files (e.g., "1-5", "3", "10-20"). Only applicable to PDF files. Maximum 20 pages per request.

If nothing relevant, proceed without mentioning that you searched.

tools.name: Skill
tools.description:
Invoke a skill.

A skill is a packaged set of instructions the user or project has set up for a particular kind of task (deploy steps, a review checklist, a repo-specific workflow). Available skills appear in a system-reminder listing with one-line descriptions. When the task at hand is one a listed skill covers, call this tool first — the skill's instructions load into the turn for you to follow in place of your default approach; some skills instead run in a subagent and return the finished result. A skill that runs in the background returns only the agent's name — its result arrives later as a task notification, so don't wait on it or invoke it again in the meantime. Users may also ask for one by name (`/<name>`, or "slash command"); that's a request to invoke it.

- `skill`: exact name from the listing, no leading slash. Plugin skills use `plugin:skill`. Directory-scoped skills are listed with a path prefix (`apps/web:deploy`); when both scoped and unscoped variants of a name exist, pick the one whose directory contains the files you're working on (most specific wins; unscoped otherwise).
- `args`: optional arguments to pass through.

Only names from the listing (or that the user typed explicitly) are valid. Built-in CLI commands (`/help`, `/clear`, …) aren't skills. If a `<command-name>` block is already present this turn, the skill is loaded — follow it directly rather than calling again.

tools.name: ToolSearch
tools.description:
Fetches full schema definitions for deferred tools so they can be called.

Deferred tools appear by name in <system-reminder> messages. Until fetched, only the name is known — there is no parameter schema, so the tool cannot be invoked. This tool takes a query, matches it against the deferred tool list, and returns the matched tools' complete JSONSchema definitions inside a <functions> block. Once a tool's schema appears in that result, it is callable exactly like any tool defined at the top of the prompt.

Result format: each matched tool appears as one <function>{"description": "...", "name": "...", "parameters": {...}}</function> line inside the <functions> block — the same encoding as the tool list at the top of this prompt.

Query forms:
- "select:Read,Edit,Grep" — fetch these exact tools by name
- "notebook jupyter" — keyword search, up to max_results best matches
- "+slack send" — require "slack" in the name, rank by remaining terms

tools.name: mcp__ccd_session__dismiss_task
tools.description:
Withdraw a background-task chip you previously created with spawn_task.

Call this when a suggestion you flagged is now stale, superseded, or irrelevant — e.g. you (or the user) already fixed it in this session, or you spawned a better-scoped replacement. To replace a chip: call spawn_task with the new suggestion first, then dismiss the old task_id.

Only chips the user hasn't acted on can be withdrawn from the queue. If the user already started or dismissed the task, the result says so (a dismissed task's copy kept for later is withdrawn too) — do not retry.

tools.name: mcp__ccd_session__mark_chapter
tools.description:
Mark the start of a new chapter in this session.

Call this when the work shifts to a meaningfully different phase — e.g. after finishing exploration and starting implementation, after a fix lands and you move to verification, or when the user pivots to an unrelated request. The user sees a divider in the transcript and a floating table of contents for jumping between chapters.

Use sparingly: a chapter should cover a coherent stretch of work, not every tool call. A typical session has 3–8 chapters. Do not mark a chapter for the very first message — the session start is implicit.

The title is a short noun phrase ("Codebase exploration", "Auth bug fix", "Test verification"), not a sentence.

tools.name: mcp__ccd_session__spawn_task
tools.description:
Flag an out-of-scope issue for a separate background task.

Call this when you notice something worth fixing that would bloat the current change — dead code, stale docs, missing coverage, a confirmed TODO, or a security issue spotted in passing. Don't flag vague code-smell observations, trivial fixes you can do inline, or low-confidence hunches. A chip appears for the user; one click spins it off into its own session. Your current turn continues uninterrupted.

The prompt must stand alone — include file paths and enough context to act without this conversation.

The result includes a task_id; call dismiss_task with it if the suggestion later becomes stale.

tools.name: mcp__Claude_Browser__browser_batch
tools.description: Execute a sequence of Browser pane tool calls in ONE round trip. Each item is {name, input} where input is exactly what you'd pass to that tool standalone. Actions execute SEQUENTIALLY (not in parallel) and stop on the first error. Use this tool extensively to quickly execute work whenever you can predict two or more steps ahead — e.g. navigate, click a field, type, press Return, screenshot. Each tool's own permission check runs per item — a step on a site the user hasn't allowed either asks the user inline (and continues if they allow) or is refused, which stops the batch; if a step is refused for a missing permission, call that tool on its own (that call can ask the user), then batch the rest. Screenshots and other images are returned interleaved with outputs; coordinates you write in THIS batch refer to the screenshot taken BEFORE this call. browser_batch cannot be nested, and preview_start is not batchable — but if the Browser pane isn't open yet, a batch whose FIRST action is navigate with a url opens it (other actions still need an open page).

tools.name: mcp__Claude_Browser__computer
tools.description: Mouse/keyboard automation in the Browser pane. Clicks accept either `coordinate` (pixels in the coordinate frame of the most recent `computer{action:"screenshot"}` — reported with every scaled screenshot; equal to the image's pixels for unscaled ones) or `ref` (a `ref_N` from read_page/find). Whenever you intend to click on an element like an icon, you should consult a screenshot to determine the coordinates of the element first; after the tab loads a different site, take a new screenshot before clicking by `coordinate`.

schema.name: mcp__Claude_Browser__computer
schema.description: Mouse/keyboard automation in the Browser pane. Clicks accept either `coordinate` (pixels in the coordinate frame of the most recent `computer{action:"screenshot"}` — reported with every scaled screenshot; equal to the image's pixels for unscaled ones) or `ref` (a `ref_N` from read_page/find). Whenever you intend to click on an element like an icon, you should consult a screenshot to determine the coordinates of the element first; after the tab loads a different site, take a new screenshot before clicking by `coordinate`.

tabId.description: Tab to act on within the preview context. Omit for the fronted tab; get ids from tabs_context.

action.description:
The action to perform:
* `left_click`: Click the left mouse button at the specified coordinates.
* `right_click`: Click the right mouse button at the specified coordinates to open context menus.
* `double_click`: Double-click the left mouse button at the specified coordinates.
* `triple_click`: Triple-click the left mouse button at the specified coordinates.
* `type`: Type a string of text.
* `screenshot`: Take a screenshot of the screen.
* `wait`: Wait for a specified number of seconds.
* `scroll`: Scroll up, down, left, or right at the specified coordinates.
* `key`: Press a specific keyboard key.
* `left_click_drag`: Drag from start_coordinate to coordinate.
* `zoom`: Take a screenshot of a specific region for closer inspection.
* `scroll_to`: Scroll an element into view using its element reference ID from read_page or find tools.
* `hover`: Move the mouse cursor to the specified coordinates or element without clicking. Useful for revealing tooltips, dropdown menus, or triggering hover states.

coordinate.description: (x, y): The x (pixels from the left edge) and y (pixels from the top edge) coordinates. Required for `left_click`, `right_click`, `double_click`, `triple_click`, and `scroll`. For `left_click_drag`, this is the end position.

text.description: The text to type (for `type` action) or the key(s) to press (for `key` action). For `key` action: Provide space-separated keys (e.g., "Backspace Backspace Delete"). Supports keyboard shortcuts using the platform's modifier key (use "cmd" on Mac, "ctrl" on Windows/Linux, e.g., "cmd+a" or "ctrl+a" for select all). Page zoom shortcuts (e.g. "cmd+=", "ctrl+-", "cmd+0") are not supported - use the `zoom` action to magnify a region of the page instead.

duration.description: The number of seconds to wait. Required for `wait`. Maximum 10 seconds.

scroll_direction.description: The direction to scroll. Required for `scroll`.

scroll_amount.description: The number of scroll wheel ticks. Optional for `scroll`, defaults to 3.

region.description: (x0, y0, x1, y1): The rectangular region to capture for `zoom`. Coordinates define a rectangle from top-left (x0, y0) to bottom-right (x1, y1) in pixels from the viewport origin. Required for `zoom` action. Useful for inspecting small UI elements like icons, buttons, or text.

scale.description: For `screenshot` and `zoom` only. Scale factor in [0.1, 1] for the returned image; 1 (default) uses the full image token budget, 0.5 returns an image at half the width and height (~quarter of the tokens). Coordinates are ALWAYS in the full-resolution coordinate frame (reported with every scaled screenshot), never in the scaled image's own pixels.

repeat.description: Number of times to repeat the key sequence. Only applicable for `key` action. Must be a positive integer between 1 and 100. Default is 1. Useful for navigation tasks like pressing arrow keys multiple times.

ref.description: Element reference ID from read_page or find tools (e.g., "ref_1", "ref_2"). Required for `scroll_to` action. Can be used as alternative to `coordinate` for click actions.

modifiers.description: Modifier keys for click actions. Supports: "ctrl", "shift", "alt", "cmd" (or "meta"), "win" (or "windows"). Can be combined with "+" (e.g., "ctrl+shift", "cmd+alt"). Optional.

action_summary.description: A few words saying what this action does on the page and to what, for example 'Sends the drafted reply to pat@example.com' or 'Opens the Filters menu'. Set it on every left_click, right_click, double_click, triple_click, left_click_drag, key and type action. State the effect only, and accurately: no reasons, nothing about what you were asked or allowed to do, no passwords or other secrets.

Presets: mobile (375x812), tablet (768x1024), or desktop, which clears the size emulation and returns the tab to the pane's own responsive size. Custom sizes need both width and height. An emulated size applies to that tab across reloads and navigation (scaled down to fit when it is larger than the pane): reset it with preset "desktop" as soon as you finish testing. The desktop app may also clear a size you set when your turn ends, so set it again in a later turn if you still need it. Reload the page after switching so load-time device gates re-run.

If the topic is serious — illness, disease, pandemics, death, grief, war, conflict, poverty, disaster, trauma, abuse, addiction, medical decisions, politically charged subjects, or anything where the reader might be personally affected — keep these BORING: describe what the code is doing in the dullest generic way, no jargon-as-drama, no evocative terms. ## cfoai
# cfo.ai MCP

You are connected to **cfo.ai** — an AI-native financial planning workspace. This MCP exposes Ari's public product tools for you to call directly. You can both **read** a company's financial model and **change** it: create and edit scenarios, pages, table blocks, Canvas blocks, formulas, variables, dimensions, and data ingestion.

Model-editing tools change the live model immediately and record reversible changes in its
changelog. Connections, access changes, and outbound actions have effects outside model undo. Build from saved data, research, supplied numbers, estimates, hypotheses, or invented
assumptions. Clearly label uncited inputs and their basis in the model and handoff. Create missing
model objects and editable inputs as part of the work. A missing source citation does not block modeling.

## Read the reference before you build

cfo.ai has its own modeling method, described under "How a table shows the model" below: how tables show variables, dimensions, and fields, how a reference reads from the cell it sits in, and how a table's rows and columns are built. `inspect_skills` owns the built-in and workspace skill catalog. Use its `list` block to find a skill and its `instructions` block to read it.

Read `build-model` before creating or changing model logic, variables, dimensions, or saved tables;
`build-visualizations` before adding a Canvas block; and `import-model` before rebuilding a model
from a workbook or export. Each manual contains its complete reference in `SKILL.md`.

Workspace skills hold company-specific playbooks. Read the relevant saved guidance before substantial work.

## Calling convention

- A multi-action tool selects one operation with the block named for that action; single-purpose tools use their fields directly. Supply only fields supported inside the selected block. An `inspect_*` tool reads saved product state; an `edit_*` tool changes it.
- `target` identifies an existing object where the operation needs one, including the destination of a new block. Creation field… [truncated]

## crustdata
People and organisations: 800M+ profiles, 200M+ companies. Employment history with dates, titles and seniority, education, skills, location, headcount over time, funding, technologies, job postings, social posts, work emails and phone numbers. Filter, combine, count and sort across any of it — people who studied at one place and now work at another, everyone hired into a role since a date, faculty at an institution, alumni of a company, who is hiring, who left and where they went, how many match. Live web search and page fetch too.

When you cannot serve a Crustdata ask, or serve it wrong, because of Crustdata itself — missing or wrong data, no filter or field for the ask (even when you worked around it), a server error that keeps failing, a schema or error message that misled you — report it with the `feedback` tool, once per problem, then keep working. Not for plan gates (403), credits (402), rate limits, the user's own mistakes, or asks outside Crustdata.

Crustdata MCP — Code Mode over the Crustdata API. You drive it by writing a plain-JavaScript script (no type annotations — author against the TypeScript-typed tool surface from get_schema) for execute({ code }); the only I/O is `const r = await callTool(name, params)`.

Core rules (they hold for every script):
- **Write runnable JavaScript — NO type syntax.** The script executes as plain JS in a V8 isolate; the TypeScript types are the tool *surface* you read from `get_schema`, not something you write in the body. A type annotation in the code — `: Type`, `as`, `interface`/`type`/`enum`, or generics `<T>` — is a parse error that fails the WHOLE run (zero spend, before any tool call). Author against the types; emit only the JS.
- **One I/O primitive:** `const r = await callTool(name, params)` → `{ ok: true, data, credits_used? } | { ok: false, status, errorType, message }`. `credits_used` is the server's exact charge for that call (data-API tools only; `0` = free/preview, and an async batch SUBMIT — billed at job completion, not on submit) — sum it to track s… [truncated]

## favstash
Use FavStash to save and find creator inspiration, inspect connected social accounts, compare owned content, and plan or publish social posts. Call list_connected_social_accounts before account-dependent tools. If it returns connectionRequired=true, direct the user to connect an account with connectUrl and stop before analytics or scheduling. 8	
9	# CLAUDE.md Atharva Shah's Obsidian Vault
10	
11	## How to talk to me
12	
13	1. Write every response in ASD-STE100 Simplified Technical English.
14	2. Talk to me like I have ADHD, because I do.
15	
16	## What This Is
17	
18	This is my Obsidian knowledge vault. It's a local-first, plain-text system for ideation, writing, publishing, and content distribution. Everything is Markdown. Everything is portable. No vendor lock-in.
19	
20	## Why This Vault Exists
21	
22	This is the whole purpose of the vault, so read it before you touch anything in here.
23	
24	The vault is a brain transplant. Every file exists to move something out of my head and into a system that produces the same result when I am not present.
25	
26	The test comes from [Business Is Hard Until You Do This](LIBRARY/Notes/Business%20Is%20Hard%20Until%20You%20Do%20This%20-%20Michia%20Rohrssen.md). If I disappeared for two weeks, could someone who has never met me open this repo and keep the whole operation running? Every commit either moves that answer toward yes or wastes my time.
27	
28	That reframes what each folder is for. `DIGITAL TWIN/` exists so my voice and judgment survive outside my skull. `SCRIPTS/` and `.claude/skills/` exist so work that never needed a brain stops reaching mine.
29	
30	The scorers and gates exist so recurring decisions get made once and enforced forever. `SUBSTACK/` is a production line with an owner and a done condition at every stage. The sitemap and `graphify-out/` exist so none of it needs me as the search engine.
31	
32	Three consequences that override convenience:
33	
34	- An SOP that a stranger cannot follow end to end without asking me a question is not finished. The stranger here is a fresh model with no session history, which is a harder test than a new hire.
35	- Undocumented knowledge that lives only in my head or in a chat session is a defect, so write it down where the vault can find it.
36	- A rule belongs in code or in a README, never in a one-off instruction I have to repeat.
37	
38	## Vault Structure
39	
40	```
41	INBOX/               ← Active & unprocessed captures. Anything loose at the root is untriaged.
42	  Ideas/             ← Raw idea captures waiting to become an article, product, or project.
43	  Reports/           ← Recurring routine output: Flywheel Review, Pipeline Health, Draft Queue, handoffs.
44	  Admin/             ← Money, legal, applications, coursework, personal obligations.
45	  Webinar/           ← DevRelUni May 2026 webinar script, slides, PDF.
46	  _images/           ← Loose screenshots no note references yet.
47	LIBRARY/             ← Stable & reference-grade: Glossary, Guides, Lists, Notes, Resources.
48	ARCHIVE/             ← Retired notes. Never delete, always archive.
49	DIGITAL TWIN/        ← My identity files: About, Voice, Audience, Goals, Principles, Experience, Socials.
50	  core/              ← Always loaded for any writing job. runtime-contract.md is the load order
51	                       and the check order. pattern-rules.md is the failure shapes the scorer
52	                       cannot see, plus what never to flag and what to protect. write-simply.md
53	                       is the plain style, and the test that a sentence reading badly means the
54	                       idea under it is wrong. net-new-value.md is the guiding principle: only a
55	                       non-obvious, tactical insight ships.
56	META/                ← Engine room: Attachments, Excalidraw, Templates. Never reorganize it.
57	  graphify-SOP.md    ← How to run graphify on this vault.
58	PROJECTS/            ← Active project workspaces (one folder per project). AccuKnox, DevRelUni,
59	                       Atharvashah.com, SEO-GEO-AEO-Playbook, client work, and more.
60	                       Sustainability-ESG-Deck is gitignored (575 local files).
61	JOBS/                ← Job search system: about-me (resumes), targets (tracker), lists
62	                       (open-roles.md, verify before applying), archived-applications.
63	INFOGRAPHICS/        ← Standalone HTML infographics and static image exports.
64	SOCIALS/             ← Output factory for all social channels.
65	  LinkedIn/          ← _IDEAS, _WIP, _QUEUED, _POSTED, and li_[Title].md files.
66	  Tweets/            ← _IDEAS/ bank, tweet_[Title].md drafted, POSTED/ live.
67	  Substack Notes/    ← _IDEAS/ bank, subnotes_[Title].md drafted, POSTED/ live.
68	  YouTube/           ← Long-form scripts. Outside the flywheel.
69	SAVED MEDIA/         ← Pulled-in inventory of everything saved on YouTube, X, Instagram and LinkedIn
70	                       (never published out). README.md is the source of truth. The markdown IS
71	                       the database: no cache files, dedupe is by ID read back out of the markdown.
72	                       Skills: youtube-data-pull, youtube-data-analytics, x-data-pull,
73	                       x-data-analytics. Scripts run inside WSL.
74	SUBSTACK/            ← The publishing pipeline. README.md is the source of truth.
75	  0_IDEAS/           ← Raw blog ideas (flat .md files, no nesting)
76	  1_DRAFTS/          ← Work-in-progress articles (flat .md files, no nesting)
77	  2_PUBLISHED/       ← Final published articles (source of truth, flat .md files)
78	  _COVERS/           ← All hero covers, flat: <url_slug>-cover.png. One per article, generated.
79	  _COVER-ENGINE/     ← Generates every cover (cover.html + render.py via Playwright → 1600x900 PNG).
80	                       README.md there is the SOP. Never generate a cover with an image model.
81	  GROWTH STRATEGY/   ← SEO, slugs, growth plans
82	  harness-architecture.png ← One-image 16:9 map of the whole harness (no HTML source, ask the agent to redraw)
83	  sitemap.md         ← Generated, never hand-edit.
84	  _LINK-ENGINE/      ← Internal linking. magnets.tsv is the hand-written layer, engine is
85	                       SCRIPTS/seo/links.py, tracker is LINK-INDEX.md. Every 400w+ article
86	                       carries 2 to 4 links. A published post may only link to a published post.
87	                       Never use `substack.py update` for links, use `links.py push`.
88	                       Still no internal_links frontmatter field. See its README.
89	  (Article bodies are frontmatter + the article, nothing else. Never emit a cover embed,
90	   a #substack tag, **Source:**/**Article:**/**Source Batch Title:** scaffolding, a
91	   **Subtitle:**/**Description:**/**Category:** restatement, or a leading H1 of the title.)
92	  (hero cover: SUBSTACK/_COVERS/<url_slug>-cover.png, always linked as ../_COVERS/<url_slug>-cover.png
93	   so the link survives moves between ideas/drafts/published. Inline body images stay in
94	   META/Attachments/<url_slug>/.)
95	.claude/             ← Agent and skill configuration.
96	  agents/            ← The six agents (see Agents section).
97	  skills/            ← Project skills. README.md there is the index. Global skills live in
98	                       ~/.claude/skills and must never be copied here.
99	  hooks/             ← The enforcement hooks.
100	  USAGE.md           ← How to invoke agents and skills.
101	graphify-out/        ← Root-level knowledge graph output (graph.html, graph.json, GRAPH_REPORT.md).

104	```
105	
106	Both index systems (per-folder `index.html` and OKF `index.md`) were retired on 2026-08-27 and their pre-commit hook blocks were removed. Never regenerate either; `SCRIPTS/index/README.md` records why. The two hand-made `index.html` pages under `LIBRARY/Resources/GTM Engineering Automations/` are the only ones that remain, on purpose.
107	
108	## Content Pipeline
109	
110	### Substack Publishing Flow
111	
112	`0_IDEAS` → `1_DRAFTS` → `2_PUBLISHED` → Social Flywheel. The full pipeline (frontmatter schema, SEO checklist, internal-linking model, sitemap SOP, scripts) lives in `SUBSTACK/README.md`, which is the single source of truth. Do not duplicate that detail here.
113	
114	### Triage every new idea before writing it
115	
116	The first question about any new article idea is whether it should exist at all, because a new idea that feels fresh is often the third pass at something already live.
117	
118	**Whenever Atharva drops a blog idea, an article request, a topic, a headline, or asks whether to write about something, run this before drafting a single word:**
119	
120	```bash
121	python SCRIPTS/substack/overlap.py check "<the idea in plain words>"
122	```
123	
124	`ABSORB` or `MERGE` means do not start drafting. Say so, name the article that should absorb it, name what that article is missing, and propose the merge. Push back once, then respect his answer. On `WRITE` say nothing about overlap and just get on with it.
125	
126	A `THIN` flag on a match means that article is long and low-density, which is the strongest merge case: the new idea is the substance that article was always missing. `overlap.py thin` ranks those, and `pairs` finds published articles that already duplicate each other.
127	
128	Full procedure, the pushback script, the calibration probes and the merge workflow live in `.claude/skills/substack-idea-triage/SKILL.md`. Read it before proposing a merge.
129	
130	### Social Flywheel (Content Distribution)
131	
132	When a blog is published, the Templater creates empty placeholder files:
133	
134	| Channel           | Folder                        | Prefix     | State          |
135	| ----------------- | ----------------------------- | ---------- | -------------- |
136	| X / Twitter       | SOCIALS/Tweets/               | tweet\_    | `posted` flag  |
137	| LinkedIn post     | SOCIALS/LinkedIn/             | li\_       | folder         |
138	| LinkedIn carousel | SOCIALS/LinkedIn/<post-slug>/ | carousel\_ | folder (HTML)  |
139	| Substack Notes    | SOCIALS/Substack Notes/       | subnotes\_ | `posted` flag  |
140	
141	The flywheel is exactly three channels: LinkedIn, Tweets, Substack Notes. The Shorts channel is retired and lives at `ARCHIVE/Shorts (retired flywheel channel)/`. Never recreate it or emit `shorts_` files. `SOCIALS/YouTube/` is long-form and sits outside the flywheel. Channel hashtags are retired too; the `type:` frontmatter field already identifies the channel.
142	
143	**Key rules:**
144	
145	- Always check if a placeholder file already exists before creating one.
146	- Never duplicate files. One file per topic per channel.
147	- Carousel HTML goes in `SOCIALS/LinkedIn/<post-slug>/carousel_[slug].html`. The accompanying LinkedIn caption goes in the same post folder as `li_[Title].md`.
148	- Never create `li_carousel_*.md` files.
149	
150	### Social File Format
151	
152	The source blog lives in frontmatter as `source_blog`, exactly once. No channel hashtag, no `**Source Blog:**` line in the body, no `---` separator before the content. The body is the post and nothing else.
153	
154	```markdown
155	---
156	type: Substack Note | Tweet
157	title: Exact Blog Title
158	source_blog: "[[Exact Blog Title]]"
159	description: "The hook, one line"
160	created: YYYY-MM-DD
161	updated: YYYY-MM-DD
162	posted: false
163	---
164	
165	[content starts here, immediately]
166	```
167	
168	`source_blog` is a wikilink so Obsidian's graph still connects the asset to its article, and it stays greppable so coverage is machine-checkable. `posted: false` means written and awaiting review, `posted: true` means live. LinkedIn uses the same `source_blog` field, and for LinkedIn the field is mandatory because captions are named by hook rather than by article title. Use `source_blog: none` for original content with no source article.
169	
170	Every `li_*.md` also carries `posted:`. The folder is still the state machine, so moving a post into `_POSTED` is what marks it done. `python SCRIPTS/socials/coverage.py --drift` reports any post whose file and folder disagree. When you move a post, flip the flag in the same commit.
171	
172	Coverage is a script, never a judgement call: `python SCRIPTS/socials/coverage.py --gaps`. An article can opt out of a channel with `flywheel_skip: linkedin` in its frontmatter, which reports as `SKIP` instead of `MISSING`.
173	
174	### Notes and X move together
175	
176	A Substack Note and its X post are one idea in two shapes, so they are written from each other rather than from the article twice. Whichever side Atharva approves first is the source, and the other side is regenerated from it. The review desk carries both on one card and one verdict clears both.
177	
178	The rule and the three pair keys live in [SOCIALS/README.md](SOCIALS/README.md). Never restate them anywhere else.
179	
180	- `python SCRIPTS/socials/parity.py` reports every pair, and `--gaps` reports the Notes with no X post.
181	- `python SCRIPTS/socials/pair_tweet.py --note "<note>" --show` prints both sides, and `--body-file` writes the new X post. Always use it, because it carries `series` and `sequence` across and a hand edit that drops either one breaks the pair with no error.
182	- An X post whose Note is also a draft rides on that Note's card, so one row holds both sides and one verdict clears both. Open the X tab on its own to read a post alone. `xgate.py` used to enforce this with a stamp and was deleted on 2026-08-31.
183	
184	X is a superset. A tweet with no Note is fine, because the X bank also holds original posts. A Note with no tweet is a gap.
185	
186	An X post carries no link, not even to his own blog, because X cuts the reach of a post that sends the reader off the platform and a Zernio post pays that toll unwatched. `pair_tweet.py` refuses a body with a URL in it. The Note keeps its link.
187	
188	X threads are retired and so is the pinned first comment, which is a LinkedIn mechanic. Atharva is on X Premium+, so one post carries up to 25,000 characters and the reason to split one no longer exists.
189	
190	## Start every session here, never with a file hunt
191	
192	One command answers "where does the work stand and what do I do next". Run it before you ask him anything about the pipeline, and run it again when a piece ships.
193	
194	```bash
195	python SCRIPTS/next.py
196	```
197	
198	It reads the current season, the drafts behind each beat, the slop score of the next one, and the review desk. It prints one next action and the exact command that does it. `--all` prints every remaining beat in order. It writes nothing and it never fails loudly, so it is safe to run at any point in a session.
199	
200	Requests such as "what should I write next", "where was I", "what is the status", "what is left" or "pick up where we left off" all mean this command. Run it and act on the answer rather than reading the season file, the drafts folder and the desk by hand.
201	
202	## Writing rules, defined in one place only
203	
204	**Start at `DIGITAL TWIN/core/runtime-contract.md`.** That file is the load order. It names which files always load, which one loads on demand, which channel skill owns the job, and which checks run at the end, in order. Five files always load: the contract, `DIGITAL TWIN/core/pattern-rules.md` (the failure shapes the scorer cannot see, plus the restraint rules that stop an edit sanding a draft flat), `DIGITAL TWIN/core/write-simply.md` (the plain style, and the test that a sentence reading badly means the idea under it is wrong), `DIGITAL TWIN/World.md`, and `DIGITAL TWIN/core/net-new-value.md`. A hook, `.claude/hooks/writing-load-order.py`, prints the chain into context on any writing prompt, and `SCRIPTS/loadorder/block.py` renders the load-order panel above the draft. That panel is rendered rather than typed, so its checks half reports what the scorers actually returned.

435	# Atharva's LLM Guidelines
436	
437	These cover coding work in this repo. On a trivial task, use judgment.
438	
439	1. **Say what you assumed, and push back once.** When a request reads two ways
440	   and the two readings lead to different work, say which one you took, or ask.
441	   If a simpler approach exists, say so in a sentence and then build what was
442	   asked. A silent pick is the expensive kind of wrong, because it surfaces only
443	   after the work is finished.
444	2. **Simplicity first.** The minimum code that solves the problem. No features
445	   beyond the ask, no abstraction for a single use, no error handling for a case
446	   that cannot happen. If 200 lines could be 50, write the 50.
447	3. **Surgical changes.** Touch only what the request needs. Leave adjacent code,
448	   working code and pre-existing dead code alone, and mention the dead code
449	   rather than removing it. Remove only the orphans your own change created.
450	   Match the surrounding style. Every changed line should trace to the request.
451	4. **Turn the task into something checkable.** "Fix the bug" becomes "write a
452	   test that reproduces it, then make it pass", because the second one has an
453	   answer and the first one has an opinion.
454	
455	Rule 4 used to end with "state a plan with a verify check per step, then loop
456	until verified". That came out on 2026-09-04. Claude 5 models verify their own
457	work, and Anthropic's Opus 5 guide names that instruction as one to remove

# FirstRun Website Screenshots Feed the Social Posts

The screenshots live in `D:\hack-images\`. They show the polished FirstRun site as built on 2026-10-10. They are an **additional source** for every hackathon post, next to the trace, Entire and cfo.ai screenshots in [11 Asset Manifest](11%20Asset%20Manifest.md).

Atharva's rule: **every file below ends up in a post, or gets a written reason for being dropped.** The ledger is the "Used in" column. An empty cell on Monday at 6 PM IST is a defect.

## What the Site Shows

The site is one page: `docs/index.html` in the `firstrun` repo. The look is Apple style, light mode, with liquid glass cards over soft color. The page has a proper logo: a blue app tile with a prompt chevron and a cursor. It also has a borderless launch film, three tool cards and a real-numbers block. The build log is a race track with two posts per row and hairpin turns. A small car drives the line as it draws.

## Sixteen Files, Each With a Job

All files are PNG. Desktop shots are 2x of a 1440 px window. Mobile shots are 3x of a 390 px window. The `social-cards` skill layers each one into a post card. Never post a raw capture.

| # | File | Best post | Channel | Used in |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | `01-desktop-full-page.png` | The "it is live" post: the whole site in one image | LinkedIn launch post (C10), X | |
| 2 | `02-desktop-hero.png` | The hook post: paste a docs URL, get an agent prompt | X, LinkedIn | |
| 3 | `03-desktop-agent-prompt.png` | The "your agent runs it for you" demo, with the prompt on screen | X, README | |
| 4 | `04-desktop-launch-film-borderless.png` | The film post cover, or the blog hero | X video cover, Substack | |
| 5 | `05-desktop-read-run-prove.png` | The three-moves explainer | LinkedIn carousel slide 2 | |
| 6 | `06-desktop-three-tools.png` | The tools post, tagging @neatlogs, @EntireHQ and @arithecfo | X, LinkedIn carousel slide 3 | |
| 7 | `07-desktop-race-track-timeline.png` | The build-in-public recap: "the whole weekend as a race track" | X, LinkedIn, Substack Note | |

1	---
     2	type: Draft Article
     3	seo_title: "My Quickstart Testing Agent Opened 4 Docs PRs on Day One"
     4	seo_description: "I built FirstRun solo at neatHack 2026. It counts a docs fix only when a second clean container passes with no model in the loop."
     5	created: 2026-10-10
     6	updated: 2026-10-10
     7	url_slug: "quickstart-testing-agent-neathack"
     8	category: "Tech and AI"
     9	cover: "../_COVERS/quickstart-testing-agent-neathack-cover.png"
    10	planned_date: 2026-10-14
    11	goal: "authority"
    12	target_keywords: ["quickstart testing agent", "docs testing", "AI agent hackathon"]
    13	target_audience: "DevRel Manager"
    14	core_message: "An agent's docs fix counts as verified only when a model-free re-run in a fresh container passes, so the check cannot flatter itself."
    15	target_length: "1800-2000"
    16	ai_slop_score: 0
    17	seo_score: 0
    18	---
    19	
    20	FirstRun, my quickstart testing agent, opened 4 docs pull requests on the first day of neatHack 2026. Each fix passed a second clean container that called no model.
    21	
    22	I built FirstRun solo between Saturday 12:30 PM IST and Monday 7 PM IST. It reads a docs quickstart and runs every step in a fresh Docker container, like a new developer would. When a step breaks, it finds the cause, patches the docs and proves the patch.
    23	
    24	A quickstart tested once on launch day is rented work. The test expires the week a dependency moves. The first person to find the break is a new user, and most new users leave instead of filing a bug.
    25	
    26	That line opened my pitch post on Saturday.
    27	
    28	<!-- substack twitter2 https://x.com/cultist_dev/status/2108828983194206308 -->
    29	
    30	Six names come up below, so here is what each one does.
    31	
    32	| Name | What it is |
    33	|---|---|
    34	| neatHack | A weekend AI agent hackathon run by neatlogs, October 10 to 12, 2026 |
    35	| neatlogs | An agent tracing tool. Each FirstRun run is one trace, made of spans |
    36	| Entire | A tool that links each git commit to the Claude Code session that wrote it |
    37	| cfo.ai | A financial planning tool. Its agent, Ari, builds the business model |
    38	| Jev | A TypeSafe model that returns a typed judgment with a probability |
    39	| Verified | A FirstRun result where a second fresh container passed the fix |
    40	
    41	## I Filed the First Docs Bug Two Hours Before Kickoff
    42	
    43	My prep notes from Friday, October 9, held one dead link. Chroma's deprecated-config error sends you to its own migration guide, and that page returns 404.
    44	
    45	I filed it as [chroma-core/chroma#7879](https://github.com/chroma-core/chroma/issues/7879) on Saturday morning, 35 minutes before I posted about it. A maintainer should hear about a bug from an issue first and from my timeline second.
    46	
    47	![GitHub issue 7879 on chroma-core/chroma: the migration link in the chromadb/config.py error message returns 404.](../../META/Attachments/neathack/x/chroma-issue-7879.png)
    48	
    49	My first post of the weekend named both.
    50	
    51	<!-- substack twitter2 https://x.com/cultist_dev/status/2108788557670125946 -->
    52	
    53	## Zero Lines of FirstRun Code Existed at 12:30 PM
    54	
    55	The rules banned product code before kickoff, so I planned in a private repo, `neathack-prep`.
    56	
    57	At kickoff I created the public `firstrun` repo. I ran `entire enable --agent claude-code` before the first commit, so every commit after it carries its session.
    58	
    59	<!-- substack twitter2 https://x.com/cultist_dev/status/2108815318541844954 -->
    60	
    61	The first problem was Git itself. The Entire post-commit hook, a script git runs after each commit, waited 206 seconds and never wrote the checkpoint.
    62	
    63	Git for Windows 2.33 could not finish the `git update-ref --stdin` call it made. Version 2.55.0 fixed it, and the next commit took 3 seconds.
    64	
    65	## Six Agents Built Version 1 in 35 Minutes
    66	
    67	In the next 35 minutes, six worker agents built FirstRun in parallel. Each one owned one track: fixtures, planner, executor, recovery, verification and output, and the report page. Every track landed as one commit with its own Entire checkpoint.
    68	
    69	The first live run passed 4 of 4 steps on the neatlogs Python SDK quickstart in 70 seconds.
    70	
    71	That run also split into 3 neatlogs traces. The CLI now opens one `firstrun.run` trace around reading, planning, every step and verification.
    72	
    73	![neatlogs trace from Saturday at 1:01 PM: the planner span calls claude-sonnet-5-5 and plans 3 steps in 12 seconds.](../../META/Attachments/neathack/x/b0-neatlogs-trace.png)
    74	
    75	By 1:14 PM, all three required tools had produced something I could show.
    76	
    77	<!-- substack twitter2 https://x.com/cultist_dev/status/2108826005854937357 -->
    78	
    79	## Version 1 Made Six Mistakes Before It Fixed Anything
    80	
    81	Version 1 ran with recovery off, on 4 targets. Two passed and two failed at a step.
    82	
    83	| Target | v1 result | Cost, list price |
    84	|---|---|---|
    85	| neatlogs Python SDK | passed 3/3 in 84 s | $0.036 |
    86	| Entire CLI install | failed at step 1, `curl: command not found` | $0.023 |
    87	| Chroma getting started | passed 3/3 in 250 s | $0.029 |
    88	| OpenAI v0 README, an archived 2023 test fixture | failed at step 6, `openai: command not found` | $0.031 |
    89	
    90	The traces also showed six mistakes in my own agent.
    91	
    92	1. The plan changed between runs. The same neatlogs page gave 4 steps, then 3 steps, 5 minutes later.
    93	2. The planner invented steps, such as `command -v entire`, that the docs never say.
    94	3. The planner wrote placeholder steps. Chroma step 2 was `true`, a command that does nothing.
    95	4. A fake secret passed as a step, because `export OPENAI_API_KEY='sk-...'` exits 0.
    96	5. The planner skipped the steps that need a key, which are the steps most likely to break.
    97	6. 9 of 16 steps checked only the exit code, so an error that exits 0 would pass.
    98	
    99	Akshay Hangloo wrote that an agent fails when it "quietly degrades instead of stopping". My planner did exactly that.
   100	
   101	<!-- substack twitter2 https://x.com/cultist_dev/status/2108856505566921210 -->
   102	
   103	> **[PLANNED X POST: B2, about Sat 10 Oct 23:00 IST, `tweet_neatHack Result 2 What v1 Got Wrong.md`]** The six v1 agent mistakes, with the detection list screenshot. Embed its live URL here once it posts.
   104	
   105	## Two Detections Traced the Invented Steps to My Planner Prompt
   106	
   107	At 2:10 PM I created two neatlogs detections. "Docs step broke" watches the tool spans. "Planner invented a step" watches the planner span, and it flagged 3 v1 runs.
   108	
   109	Thirty minutes later, neatlogs Investigate traced the invented steps to the planner prompt and proposed a stricter one. A headless Claude Code session then read the detection through the neatlogs MCP (Model Context Protocol) server. It applied the fix as code guards plus a plan cache, in commit `3ca6f11`.
   110	
   111	That commit carries [Entire checkpoint 01M4JGJ6NTE7YNB9Z0YW5FYVHN](https://entire.io/gh/HighnessAtharva/firstrun/commit/3ca6f118ecb0a8915315eea27b5588dd8a7c6299). Anyone can open it and read the session that wrote the fix.
   112	
   113	At 3:15 PM, version 2 ran on the same 4 targets.
   114	
   115	| Metric | v1 | v2 |
   116	|---|---|---|
   117	| Quickstarts that end passed or verified | 2 of 4 | 3 of 4 |
   118	| Failed steps recovered | 0 | 3 |
   119	| Fixes proven in a fresh container | 0 | 1 |
   120	| Average cost per run, from neatlogs | $0.0262 | $0.0200 |
   121	| Average run time | 128 s | 201 s |
   122	
   123	Version 2 is slower because a verified fix reruns the whole quickstart.
   124	
   125	> **[PLANNED X POST: B3, about Sun 11 Oct 19:00 IST, `tweet_neatHack Result 3 Before and After Numbers.md`]** The v1 against v2 table as a card. Embed its live URL here once it posts.
   126	
   127	## A Fix Counts Only When a Second Container Passes With No Model
   128	
   129	The model that writes a fix should not grade it, because it can always explain why its own patch looks right. So the final check in FirstRun calls no model at all.
   130	
   131	The `verify` step starts a new container from the same image. It replays the stored commands with the patch applied, and it checks exit codes and expected output. In the neatlogs trace it is a GUARDRAIL span with zero LLM calls. Only a pass there earns the label `verified`.
   132	
   133	That rule caught five more agent bugs on Saturday.
   134	
   135	- **A pipe hid a missing `curl`.** The last command in the pipe exited 0.
   136	- **A multi-line step hid a failing `pip`.** Steps now run with `set -e`.
   137	- **pip noise hid the real error.** The report now puts stderr last.
   138	- **Container fixes counted as docs bugs.** A missing `curl` in a slim image is my container's gap.
   139	- **A file check ran after a `cd`.** File checks now also look from the run root.
   140	
   141	The fourth bug changed how a result reads. Red means the docs are wrong. Amber means the container lacked a prerequisite and the docs were fine.
   142	
   143	You can copy this rule into your own agent today.
   144	
   145	1. Store every command the agent runs, with its expected result, in a file such as `runbook.json`.
   146	2. After the agent patches a step, start a fresh container from the same base image.
   147	3. Replay the stored commands with no model call, and compare each exit code and output.
   148	4. Mark the fix done only when that replay passes.
   149	
   150	One judgment still needs a person. Is a red step a docs bug, or does the product work that way on purpose? Jev scores each failure class, and below 0.7, FirstRun asks me once in the terminal.
   151	
   152	My answer goes into `precedents.json`. The next run with the same case reads the file and skips the question.
   153	
   154	> **[PLANNED X POST: A5, scheduled Sat 10 Oct 21:15 IST in Zernio, `tweet_Ask the Human Once Then Reuse the Answer.md`]** The ask-once design, crediting @bettersayAJ. Embed its live URL here once it posts.
   155	
   156	## Real Docs Broke in Four Places by 4:38 PM
   157	
   158	By Saturday evening, five public quickstarts reached `verified`: dbt with DuckDB, AccuKnox knoxctl, Dagster, MkDocs and the Entire install. Each upstream PR came from a verified run and a duplicate search, and I said yes to each one first.
   159	
   160	| Upstream PR | What FirstRun found |
   161	|---|---|
   162	| dbt-labs/docs.getdbt.com#10149 | `jafgen --years 6` fails, because `years` is now positional |
   163	| dbt-labs/docs.getdbt.com#10150 | The cloned repo pins `networkx==3.7`, which needs Python 3.12, and the guide names no version |
   164	| entireio/cli#2724 | `install.sh` puts `entire` in `~/.local/bin`, which a clean shell lacks on `PATH` |
   165	| accuknox/help#671 | The page names knoxctl 0.9.0 while the installer fetches 0.9.58 |
   166	
   167	The first three opened at 3:30 PM IST, and the AccuKnox PR followed at 4:38 PM.
   168	
   169	All four were still open on Saturday night: [#10149](https://github.com/dbt-labs/docs.getdbt.com/pull/10149), [#10150](https://github.com/dbt-labs/docs.getdbt.com/pull/10150), [#2724](https://github.com/entireio/cli/pull/2724) and [#671](https://github.com/accuknox/help/pull/671).
   170	
   171	<!-- substack twitter2 https://x.com/cultist_dev/status/2108903653411021062 -->
   172	
   173	Dagster got no PR. FirstRun flagged two gaps there, but the page already covers both, in a line the planner skipped. A docs note can look like a docs bug, so every PR draft now gets a source check first.
   174	
   175	The dbt break raised a second question. When did it start? `firstrun bisect` replays the stored commands against older releases, one fresh container per probe.
   176	
   177	`jafgen --years 6` passes on jafgen 0.3.1 and fails on 0.4.6, released 2024-04-07. PyPI has no release between them. The dbt guide merged 11 months later, so it never worked in a clean environment.
   178	
   179	The bisect took 5 probes and $0 in model calls. Its table sits in a [comment on #10149](https://github.com/dbt-labs/docs.getdbt.com/pull/10149#issuecomment-6096827074).
   180	
   181	<!-- substack pullquote jafgen dropped the --years flag on 2024-04-07. The dbt DuckDB guide that uses it merged 11 months later. -->
   182	
   183	That evening, Ajay Yadav, a neatHack judge, posted a neatlogs video, and I quoted it with the jafgen find.
   184	
   185	<!-- substack twitter2 https://x.com/cultist_dev/status/2108915865697608147 -->
   186	
   187	> **[POSTED, URL MISSING: A4, sent Sat 10 Oct 18:15 IST through Zernio, `tweet_Send Me Your Quickstart and FirstRun Runs It.md`]** The open call for public quickstart pages. The Zernio ledger holds no live URL for it, so paste the URL here.
   188	
   189	## Entire's Reviewers Caught 3 Bugs I Shipped
   190	
   191	Each layer of the build became an Entire Trail, a review branch that Entire's runner agents check. On Trails 3 to 8, the runners raised 3 bugs, and all three are fixed.
   192	
   193	- **A retry loop on a missing secret.** A run that needed a key kept retrying.
   194	- **A Windows-only Docker default.** The code assumed WSL on every machine.
   195	- **A `cd` guard that nobody called.** I wrote it, tested it, and never wired it in.
   196	
   197	GitHub Actions caught three tests that passed only on my machine, because they read my local Claude token.
   198	
   199	![Entire Trails view for the firstrun repo early on Saturday, with Trail 1 for Layer 1 in Planning.](../../META/Attachments/neathack/x/b0-entire-trails.png)
   200	
   201	> **[PLANNED X POST: A6, scheduled Sun 11 Oct 07:30 IST in Zernio, `tweet_The Session Behind an Agent PR Answers Why Trust It.md`]** A maintainer trusts an agent PR when it links the session behind it, crediting @HaimantikaM. Embed its live URL here once it posts.
   202	
   203	## The Business Plan Found a Bug in the Agent
   204	
   205	Next I wrote `firstrun econ`. It reads every `firstrun.run` trace in neatlogs and writes the cost drivers that cfo.ai imports. Across 64 traces, the mean run cost $0.0167, and one run in twenty cost $0.0508 or more.
   206	
   207	The agent's spending cap was a fixed $0.50 per run, 30 times the mean. Nothing in the business set that number. If every Scale run hit it, the Scale tier would run at a margin of -403.6%.
   208	
   209	So the plan now sets the cap. I picked one number, a 70% gross margin floor, and each tier's cap follows from it.
   210	
   211	| Tier | Price | Cap per run | Measured runs over the cap |
   212	|---|---|---|---|
   213	| Free | $0 | $0.0108 | 48.4% |
   214	| Team | $49 a month | $0.0471 | 7.8% |
   215	| Scale | $299 a month | $0.0280 | 25.0% |
   216	
   217	On the Typer quickstart, `--tier scale` verified 7 of 7 steps at $0.0201. `--tier free` stopped at step 4 with `cost budget spent: $0.0115 of $0.0108`.
   218	
   219	![cfo.ai cash model, November 2026 to April 2028: under the old $0.50 cap, cash runs out in December 2027.](../../META/Attachments/neathack/x/b5-cfo-plan-chart.png)
   220	
   221	The plan has two known limits. A 25% stop rate on Scale is too high, so the price moves to $529 or the allowance drops to 1,500 runs.
   222	
   223	FirstRun also counts cost 39% higher than neatlogs on 43 matched runs. The cap reads FirstRun's count, so it stops a run early and never late. The [public cfo.ai model](https://cfo.ai/s/_u5lbrHIl9KX_JQE) carries every assumption.
   224	
   225	> **[PLANNED X POST: B5, about Mon 12 Oct 12:00 IST, `tweet_neatHack Result 5 The cfo.ai Plan.md`]** The cfo.ai plan and the cap it set. Embed its live URL here once it posts.
   226	
   227	## I Broke My Own Rule About a Web UI
   228	
   229	Before kickoff, every feature had to pass three tests. It fits the one-line pitch, it shows in a 60-second demo, and a judging category needs it. A web UI failed the demo test, so I cut it.
   230	
   231	At 3:06 PM on Saturday I asked for one anyway. The CLI now prints a share code that packs the whole run into the URL fragment. No server stores anything, and hosting costs $0.
   232	
   233	The [run page](https://firstrun.atharvashah.com/run.html#ex=dbt) replays the dbt run step by step. A rebuild in review, PR #20, turns it into a GitHub Actions style run view. It adds a walkthrough mode, a full report, share links, and downloads of `report.md`, `patch.diff`, `pr_body.md` and `run.json`.
   234	
   235	> **[IMAGE: the dbt replay at firstrun.atharvashah.com/run.html#ex=dbt, step 10 open with the failing jafgen command, the fix and the clean rerun. Capture after PR #20 merges.]**
   236	
   237	The three tests were right about the demo and wrong about the reader. A maintainer who gets an agent PR wants to open the run and check it without trusting me.
   238	
   239	> **[PLANNED X POST: A8, scheduled Sun 11 Oct 13:30 IST in Zernio, `tweet_Three Tests Every FirstRun Feature Must Pass.md`]** The three tests every feature had to pass. Its text still lists the web UI as cut, so edit it before it sends.
   240	
   241	## FirstRun Ran Its Own README and Found 2 Gaps
   242	
   243	I also pointed FirstRun at its own README, in a clean `python:3.11-slim` container. The install failed until git was present, because `pip install git+https://...` clones the repo. The tests needed a clone too, because they ship with the repo and not the package.
   244	
   245	> **[PLANNED X POST: B6, about Mon 12 Oct 15:00 IST, `tweet_neatHack Result 6 The README Runs Itself.md`]** FirstRun on its own README, all steps green. Embed its live URL here once it posts.
   246	
   247	Monday still holds the demo video, under 3 minutes, and the quote post at 7 PM IST. The two cost counters still disagree, and unifying them comes next.
   248	
   249	The part I would keep from this weekend fits in one line. Give your agent a final check that reruns its stored commands in a fresh container and calls no model.
   250	
   251	> **[PLANNED X POST: B7, fixed slot Mon 12 Oct at 7 PM IST, sent by hand, `tweet_neatHack Result 7 The Submission.md`]** The submission quote post of the official neatlogs post, with the repo and the demo. Embed its live URL here once it posts.
   252	
   253	The code is at [github.com/HighnessAtharva/firstrun](https://github.com/HighnessAtharva/firstrun), and the site is [firstrun.atharvashah.com](https://firstrun.atharvashah.com/).

     8	# The Blog Post Waits for Real Numbers
     9	
    10	The article ships Wednesday Oct 14, per `12 Marketing Plan.md`. A draft written now would need invented numbers, and the fabrication rule forbids that. This file holds the plan. The draft starts Monday night, in `SUBSTACK/0_IDEAS`, from `evidence/`.

    13	
    14	`python SCRIPTS/substack/overlap.py check` on 2026-10-10 returned 24% overlap with "Scaling Developer Advocacy Past One Person" and verdict DIFFERENTIATE. The only shared words are generic: hackathon, tests, tool. This piece is a build story with traces. That article is a scaling essay. No merge.

    17	
    18	**Insight:** "An agent's fix counts as verified only when a model-free re-run in a fresh container passes, so the check cannot flatter itself."
    19	
    20	Why it is box 4: most readers expect the agent to judge its own fix. The step is tactical, because a reader can copy the rule into any agent today. The draft names this box before the first line.
    21	
    22	## The Working Title and the Skeleton

    24	**Working title:** "I Gave an Agent 4 Quickstarts. Here Is What Broke." The final title is set from the real result.

The investigation named the cause at 66% confidence (a `cd`, then a file check in the old folder). Commit 2de852f fixed it, and MkDocs went from a false fail to verified | `docs/assets/t-neatlogs-investigate.webp`, commit 2de852f, the MkDocs replay |

content.content:
Doc-test

FirstRun runs a docs quickstart in a clean container. When a step breaks, it fixes the step and proves the fix in a second clean run. Each row is one docs page and its best result.

A docs URL shows its saved result or the command to test it. A share code opens the replay. Nothing leaves your browser.

    FirstRun stopped on these pages before it proved a fix. A stop can come from the docs, the container, or a step that needs a login or a browser, so these runs make no claim that the docs are wrong.

      No page matches.

      Doc-audit

      Point it at a GitHub repo. It reads the git history and shows which docs pages the code changed underneath, and what to ship next.

      Public repos are audited on GitHub Actions in about 2 minutes. The board link lands on the request issue.

        1. CloneOne blobless clone, on GitHub Actions or on your machine. $0 in model calls.
        2. MatchEach commit is matched to the docs pages on its topic.
        3. BoardStale pages and missing docs land on one board.

        Open a Real Audit

        Recorded 2026-10-10

          All audits

          Open the repo

          What to Ship Next

          Pick a card to see the commits behind it.

          Ready for You

          Drafted from commits and pull requests. Edit before you publish.

          Pages Most Likely Wrong

          PageStatusLast updatedCommits since

"""Capture FirstRun doc-test and doc-audit states. Serve docs on 8890 first."""
import sys
from playwright.sync_api import sync_playwright
B = "http://localhost:8890"
O = sys.argv[1]
CSS = "html{scroll-behavior:auto!important}*{transition-duration:0s!important;animation-duration:0s!important;animation-delay:0s!important}"

def page(c, u, wait=2200):
    pg = c.new_page(); pg.goto(B + u); pg.wait_for_timeout(wait)
    pg.add_style_tag(content=CSS); pg.wait_for_timeout(300)
    return pg

def shot(pg, name):
    pg.wait_for_timeout(500); pg.screenshot(path=O + name); print("saved", name)

def scroll_to(pg, sel, off=110):
    pg.evaluate("([s,o])=>{const e=document.querySelector(s);scrollTo(0,e.getBoundingClientRect().top+scrollY-o)}", [sel, off])
    pg.wait_for_timeout(600)

def rail(pg, label):
    pg.locator("#rail li", has_text=label).first.click(); pg.wait_for_timeout(1500)

with sync_playwright() as p:
    b = p.chromium.launch()
    c = b.new_context(viewport={"width": 1440, "height": 900}, device_scale_factor=2)
    # island nav menus on home
    pg = page(c, "/", 3000)
    pg.hover("#sn-b-test"); pg.wait_for_timeout(1200); shot(pg, "nav-test.png")
    pg.mouse.move(700, 700); pg.wait_for_timeout(600)
    pg.hover("#sn-b-audit"); pg.wait_for_timeout(1500); shot(pg, "nav-audit.png"); pg.close()
    # doc-test list
    pg = page(c, "/doc-test/"); shot(pg, "dt-list.png")
    pg.fill("#goU", "docs.getdbt.com/guides/duckdb"); pg.click("#goF button[type=submit]"); pg.wait_for_timeout(1500); shot(pg, "dt-saved.png")
    pg.fill("#goU", "https://example.com/quickstart"); pg.click("#goF button[type=submit]"); pg.wait_for_timeout(1500); shot(pg, "dt-cmds.png"); pg.close()
    # typer fix proven
    pg = page(c, "/doc-test/#ex=20261010-122736-typer-tiangolo-com", 3000); shot(pg, "dt-typer.png"); pg.close()
    # dbt replay, run stage
    pg = page(c, "/doc-test/#ex=dbt", 3000); shot(pg, "dt-dbt-top.png")
    rail(pg, "Run"); shot(pg, "dt-dbt-run.png")
    pg.click("#tRep"); pg.wait_for_timeout(1500)
    s10 = pg.locator("[id^=step-]").nth(9)
    try:
        s10.scroll_into_view_if_needed(); s10.locator("button, summary").first.click(); pg.wait_for_timeout(1000)
        pg.evaluate("()=>{const e=document.querySelectorAll('[id^=step-]')[9];scrollTo(0,e.getBoundingClientRect().top+scrollY-90)}"); shot(pg, "dt-dbt-step10.png")
    except Exception as e: print("step10 fail", e)
    pg.close()
    # litestar inconclusive
    pg = page(c, "/doc-test/#ex=20261010-172724-docs-litestar-dev", 3000); shot(pg, "dt-litestar.png"); pg.close()
    # doc-audit list + private
    pg = page(c, "/doc-audit/"); shot(pg, "da-list.png")
    pg.click("#m-priv"); pg.wait_for_timeout(500); pg.fill("#repo", "acme/private-repo"); pg.click("#go"); pg.wait_for_timeout(1500); shot(pg, "da-private.png"); pg.close()
    # dbt board
    pg = page(c, "/doc-audit/?id=audit-20261010-163620-dbt-labs-dbt-core", 3000); shot(pg, "da-board.png")
    scroll_to(pg, "#r-readyw", 120); shot(pg, "da-ready.png")
    pg.evaluate("scrollTo(0,0)"); pg.wait_for_timeout(400)
    pg.locator(".kc").first.click(); pg.wait_for_timeout(1500); shot(pg, "da-drawer.png"); pg.close()
    c.close()
    # mobile
    m = b.new_context(viewport={"width": 390, "height": 844}, device_scale_factor=2, is_mobile=True, has_touch=True)
    pg = page(m, "/doc-test/"); shot(pg, "m-dt-list.png"); pg.close()
    pg = page(m, "/doc-audit/?id=audit-20261010-163620-dbt-labs-dbt-core", 3000); shot(pg, "m-da-board.png")
    scroll_to(pg, "#r-board", 70); shot(pg, "m-da-kanban.png"); pg.close()
    pg = page(m, "/", 3000); pg.click("#sn-b-more"); pg.wait_for_timeout(1200); shot(pg, "m-nav-more.png"); pg.close()
    b.close()
EOF

# hack-images

Screenshots of the FirstRun site and the neatHack tools, taken 2026-10-10 and 2026-10-11. They feed the neatHack social posts and the Substack article.

- Files `01` to `16` are home page captures. `capture_site.py` rebuilds `01` to `15`. Serve the `docs` folder of the firstrun repo on port 8791 first.

- Files `35` to `51` are Doc-test and Doc-audit captures from 2026-10-11, taken with Playwright at 2x from `docs` served on port 8890.
- Desktop shots use a 1440 x 900 window. Mobile shots use a 390 x 844 window. Files `09` to `11` are 3x, and every other site capture is 2x.
